rationale: Interpreted the successor receipt, which adds the request shape the earlier revision lacked and changes what the account can say about the damaged follower. The second execution (receipt 3448bd1c64244c3b884b24c7bad8a8bf) repeats the conflict, the whole-log append and then sends the append a leader sends while its nextIndex is still one past the follower's stale last index, a single entry 4 behind previous index 3: the follower accepted it with Success true even though its store held no entry 2 or 3, so the store now carries index 4 above a gap, while the whole-log append that would close the gap was refused in the same run; the control accepted both and ended with a contiguous store. I rewrote the account around both receipts, recorded the acceptance above the gap as a Fact with its indices, and left the live-leader walk and the vote consequence as the open discriminator.

interpretations.rationale: The question asks whether the follower keeps an in-memory last log index its store no longer holds and whether ordinary AppendEntries can bring it back; both halves are answered, and the answer to the second is now sharper than refusal alone. After the conflicting append with the store failure armed (receipt 3448bd1c64244c3b884b24c7bad8a8bf, injected case, conflict index 1) the node's last log index was 3 while its store held only index 1 and no longer held index 2, and it answered Success false with that stale index. Ordinary AppendEntries then go two ways. The whole-log append from index 1 - the shape the leader's builder produces once its rejections have walked nextIndex back to one - was refused (index 2, Success false, store still at index 1), because the conflict loop trusts the stale in-memory index, looks the missing entry up in the store, misses and returns. But the shape a leader sends while its nextIndex is still one past that stale index, a single entry 4 behind previous index 3, was accepted with Success true (index 3): the store now holds index 4 above a gap at 2 and 3, the node's last log index is 4, and the leader reading that response would take the peer as caught up. The control accepted both shapes and kept a contiguous store from 1 to 4 (indices 5 to 7), so the injected failure is what produced the gap. The mechanism is the same source path in all three phases: the abort returns before setLastLog, the in-memory last log stays ahead of the store, the conflict loop treats any index above it as new without reading the store, and the abort also refreshes no contact. What remains source-read rather than measured is a live leader walking its nextIndex down and the effect of the stale index on the node's own vote claims, which the vote path takes from the same in-memory fields.
counterevidence: The trigger is a store error on one RPC, and the library's leader path treats the same error as a reason to step down and to fail the caller, so a store error may be intended as a condition that takes a node out of service rather than one a follower must survive in place.

The requests in the receipt are supplied by the probe; the leader's own builder produces those shapes at the corresponding nextIndex values, but no live leader walked its nextIndex down in this receipt and the interval that takes is unmeasured.

The state need not be permanent: the snapshot path fires once the leader's log no longer holds the follower's nextIndex, and a restart rebuilds the in-memory last log from the store, after which the gap would be visible.

In this three-entry probe the gap covers only user entries; nothing here shows what the leader does with the acceptance beyond its own bookkeeping, and the control shows the same requests are handled normally when the store does not fail.
limitations: Two executions of the same lineage, eight events in the latest, two cases and three request shapes each; the outcomes were uniform but the probe does not vary the failure point, the number of retries, or the timeouts, which were two seconds for heartbeat, election and lease.

The account depends on a supplied fault - a store whose StoreLogs returns an injected error for the append that follows a truncation in the same RPC - and says nothing about torn writes, a lost acknowledged write, or a monotonic store.

The contract is disputed in the counterevidence above: the same store error leads the leader path to step down, so an operator may be expected to restart the node instead of relying on in-place repair.

The consequence of the gapped store beyond this node - whether a leader counts the acknowledgement, what happens if the node campaigns or is asked for those entries - is inferred from the source and not measured.

knowledge.assertion: The aborts that can follow a suffix deletion in the same RPC return without advancing the in-memory last log, so the follower keeps an index its store has lost.
A node judges and claims elections with its in-memory last log, so the stale claim would also be what it offers as a candidate.

knowledge.statement: A follower that was left with an in-memory last log index ahead of its store rejects the append that would repair it and accepts the append that extends it, so its store ends up holding an entry above a gap while it answers the leader with success. In the executed probe the damaged case refused the whole-log append with previous index zero and Success false, then accepted a single entry 4 behind previous index 3 with Success true, ending with last log index 4 over a store that no longer held index 2 or 3; the control case accepted both and ended with a contiguous store through index 4.
knowledge.conditions: One in-process raft node with an in-memory log store wrapped by a store that failed exactly one StoreLogs call on the append that followed a truncated suffix, driven by three to four AppendEntries requests sent directly to its handler; two-second heartbeat, election and lease timeouts; no live leader, no snapshot activity and a non-monotonic in-memory store.
